note: Abstract says order can be the difference between near state-of-the-art and random guess and that this is present across model sizes, even the largest. Record wording (published work reports order/choice effects, persisting across model sizes in those studies, model-dependent) is hedged and matches. The 'choice' part rests on other literature, not this paper alone.

Page says consolidating related operations into fewer, more capable tools reduces selection ambiguity; detailed descriptions are 'by far the most important factor in tool performance'; strict: true enables schema validation. Record points (reduce overlap, when-to-use descriptions, strict mode enforces shape) are consistent. Page itself defers strict-mode mechanics to another page; record's 'enforces shape, not existence' is a reasonable inference, not a quote.

Willison defines the three legs (private data, untrusted content, external communication), says failing to understand this lets an attacker steal data, and says the only safe route is to avoid the combination entirely. Record's three-ingredient explanation and 'cut a leg' match.

Fetch returned OWASP LLM06 guidance on minimum extensions/permissions, executing in the user's context (user authorisation/scope tracking), human-in-the-loop for high-impact actions, and authorisation in downstream systems rather than by the LLM. The exact heading text was not echoed verbatim by the summariser but the substance is present. Matches record's design bullets.

Abstract names position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and reports GPT-4-class judges reaching over 80% agreement with humans. Record only claims judges can show verbosity and other biases with magnitude depending on judge and task; this is supported (the 80% claim is not used in the record).

Abstract: RAG consistently outperforms unsupervised fine-tuning for existing and new knowledge; LLMs struggle to learn new facts via fine-tuning. Record says 'retrieval often beat... struggled... setup-dependent', which is a safe narrowing.

Hu et al. abstract is accurate for the entry text (frozen weights, trainable low-rank matrices, far fewer trainable parameters, no extra inference latency vs adapters), but the record's only LoRA claim (LoRA learned less but forgot less than full fine-tuning on code/maths) comes from Biderman et al., not Hu et al. Hu supports only the generic idea that LoRA/adapter tuning is a lightweight alternative to full fine-tuning.
narrowed_supports: Abstract: LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and trains injected low-rank matrices, greatly reducing trainable parameters; supports only that adapter-based tuning is a lighter-weight alternative to full-parameter tuning, not the forgetting trade-off claim.

note: Abstract: almost all knowledge is learned in pretraining and only limited instruction-tuning data (1,000 curated prompts/responses) is needed for high-quality output. Record hedges 'argue... in their setup' (11-2) and 'argues a small, carefully curated set can be enough' for style/format (11-6); consistent. The 1,000 figure was in my earlier-known abstract but my fetch only confirmed the pretraining-knowledge and few-examples statements.

Abstract: LLM-integrated apps blur data/instructions, attackers plant prompts in retrieved content, and effective defenses are currently lacking (as of 2023). Supports record's premise that injected text can influence the model and 'none is complete'. Does not support the specific five-layer controls, which are the record's own design advice. Note the 'lacking' statement is dated 2023.

Record cites Greshake for 'applications put instructions and data in one channel'; abstract says LLM-integrated applications 'blur the line between data and instructions'. Matches. Source covers indirect injection only, so it does not back the closing remark that neither category (incl. jailbreaks) has a complete defence.

Fetch confirmed: batching needs many requests; KV cache memory wasted via fragmentation and redundant duplication, limiting batch size; PagedAttention inspired by OS virtual memory/paging; vLLM. My fetch did not surface the 'huge and grows and shrinks dynamically' or 'near-zero waste' wording (a re-check was blocked by a session limit), so those two fragments are unverified by me.
narrowed_supports: Abstract (confirmed): inefficient KV cache management wastes memory through fragmentation and redundant duplication, limiting batch size; PagedAttention is inspired by OS virtual memory and paging.

note: Section 1.1/3.3.1: lower bound on hallucination rate based on fraction of prompts (facts) appearing once (singleton rate); example '20% singleton birthdays -> at least 20% hallucination' for base models. Record's 'facts that appear once or never are the hardest to learn reliably' is a weaker, safe paraphrase (the paper's bound is a model-based lower bound for base models, not a literal floor for every model).

SelfCheckGPT premise: if the LLM knows a concept, sampled responses are similar and consistent; hallucinated facts tend to diverge. Matches record's 'disagreement among samples is a useful warning... a model that does not know tends to scatter'. Record adds its own caveats (consistent errors, cost), which are unsourced but hedged.
